claims.text: The FeNiCrCoCu coating initially has a defect-free or low-defect FCC single-crystal structure.
Above 900 K, thermal activation produces Shockley partial dislocations and extensive stacking-fault formation in FeNiCrCoCu.
High thermal energy above 900 K unlocks Lomer-Cottrell locks.
Unlocking Lomer-Cottrell locks causes annihilation of dislocation networks and dislocation starvation.
Local amorphization or severe lattice disorder begins when stacking-fault density exceeds a critical threshold.
Local amorphization or lattice disorder reduces the coating's ability to sustain shear stress.
Plasticity above 900 K changes from dislocation-mediated deformation to disordered, fluid-like flow beneath the indenter.
Disordered flow causes a sharp hardness decrease.
Adhesive wear and material transfer to the Cu matrix cause the friction coefficient to spike.
FeNiCrCoCu has high stacking-fault energy at elevated temperatures.
The high stacking-fault energy of FeNiCrCoCu promotes cross-slip and dislocation annihilation.
At high temperature, thermal energy overcomes the Peierls barrier and facilitates Lomer-Cottrell lock unlocking, as allegedly observed in PMC8398136.
High-temperature deformation in FeNiCrCoCu produces rapid dislocation annihilation and stacking-fault collapse.
CoCrFeMnNi undergoes dynamic recrystallization under the conditions represented by PMC7229066.
The single-crystal structure and high stacking-fault energy of FeNiCrCoCu favor amorphization rather than grain-boundary formation.
At 300 K and 600 K, dislocation pile-up and work hardening produce high hardness and low friction.
Above 900 K, the friction coefficient increases by more than 50% and wear resistance decreases by more than 80%.
At 1200 K, the coating exhibits near-fluid behavior with minimal indentation resistance.
Standard FCC HEAs remain mechanically stable through dislocation hardening up to approximately 0.5 times their melting temperature.
At 1200 K, interdiffusion with the Cu matrix could alter the proposed thermal-disorder mechanism.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says stacking-fault-mediated disorder causes the friction spike and wear loss, so eliminating the spike when stacking faults are suppressed would support that causal account. The falsification rule incorrectly labels that result as falsification. Persistence of the spike despite suppression would instead falsify or weaken the proposed stacking-fault-dependent mechanism.

The event sequence invokes extensive stacking-fault accumulation until a critical density is exceeded, while the mechanism also invokes rapid stacking-fault collapse. The temporal relationship between accumulation, collapse, and amorphization is not specified, leaving the proposed mediator sequence internally ambiguous.
